extracted.intended_audience: federal agency analysts and rulewriters preparing regulatory analyses (RIAs) and supporting materials for OMB review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing regulatory analyses (benefit-cost and cost-effectiveness) and standardized accounting statements to support major and other Federal rulemakings under Executive Order 12866 and related authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key elements of a regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A good regulatory analysis should include: (1) a statement of the need for the proposed action, (2) an examination of alternative approaches, and (3) an evaluation of the benefits and costs—quantitative and qualitative—of the proposed action and the main alternatives identified by the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include discussion of non-quantified as well as quantified benefits and costs; present a summary of benefit and cost estimates for each alternative, including qualitative and non-monetized factors; provide an executive summary and a standardized accounting statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate the need for federal regulatory action
rubrics_metrics.description: Before recommending Federal regulatory action, an agency must demonstrate that the proposed action is necessary, describing the specific authority for the action, the extent of discretion available, and the regulatory instruments that might be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain whether the action addresses a significant market failure (qualitatively and, where feasible, quantitatively) or meets another compelling social purpose; show that government intervention is likely to do more good than harm; discuss strengths and limitations of intangible rationales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and define the baseline for comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify a baseline. Benefits and costs are defined in comparison with a clearly stated alternative, normally a 'no action' baseline; comparisons to a 'next best' alternative are also useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State explicitly what the world will be like if the proposed rule is not adopted and use that baseline consistently when measuring incremental benefits and costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider a comprehensive set of alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory analysis must examine alternative approaches and consider reasonable alternatives reflecting statutory discretion as well as other options that modify attributes of the regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider alternatives including: different choices defined by statute, different compliance dates, different enforcement methods, different degrees of stringency, different requirements by firm size or region, performance standards versus design standards, market-oriented approaches, and informational measures. Eliminate some alternatives via preliminary analysis but retain a manageable set for detailed evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate benefits and costs (quantified and qualitative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the benefits and costs—quantitative and qualitative—of the proposed action and main alternatives identified; quantify and monetize where feasible, and discuss non-quantified outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how actions required by the rule are linked to expected benefits; identify undesirable side-effects and ancillary benefits; present both quantified/monetized estimates and qualitative descriptions of non-monetized effects, indicating which non-quantified effects are most important and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Benefit-Cost Analysis (BCA) where feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Where all benefits and costs can be quantified and expressed in monetary units, use benefit-cost analysis to indicate the most efficient alternative (one that generates the largest net benefits to society).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure incremental benefits and costs, identify alternative that maximizes net benefits; avoid using benefit-cost ratios alone as they can be misleading; when some benefits/costs cannot be monetized, exercise professional judgment and consider threshold analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Cost-Effectiveness Analysis (CEA) for health/safety rulemakings
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare a CEA for major rulemakings where the primary benefits are improved public health and safety and a valid effectiveness measure can be developed; perform BCA for major health and safety rulemakings when valid monetary values can be assigned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer final outcomes (lives saved, life-years saved) to intermediate outputs; construct cost and effectiveness measures consistently; avoid relying on average cost-effectiveness—use incremental cost-effectiveness analysis; where multiple outcomes exist, either weight into a single index or perform BCA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of non-quantified benefits and costs (threshold analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: When not all important benefits and costs can be monetized, indicate which non-quantified effects are likely important and carry out threshold/break-even analysis to evaluate their significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Threshold analysis answers how small the non-quantified benefits could be (or how large non-quantified costs would need to be) before net benefits are zero; clearly explain which non-quantified factors justify consideration and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A good analysis is transparent: it should be possible for a qualified third party to see how estimates and conclusions were derived, including assumptions, time horizon, discount rates, data sources, and models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific references to all data sources, appendices documenting models where necessary, results of formal sensitivity/uncertainty analyses, and an executive summary. State all assumptions explicitly and provide citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity analysis and exploration of uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide sensitivity analysis to reveal whether, and to what extent, results are sensitive to plausible changes in assumptions and numeric inputs; use sensitivity analysis to find 'switch points' where rankings or net benefits change sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary one variable at a time or combinations; if net benefits or rankings change under plausible assumptions, conduct further analysis; for complex or high-stakes rules, apply formal probabilistic analysis (simulation, expert judgment) and present results clearly (graphs/tables).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal probabilistic analysis for high-impact rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply formal probabilistic analyses (e.g., Monte Carlo simulations with expert elicitation) for complex rules with large, multiple uncertainties, and such analysis is required for rules exceeding the $1 billion annual threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify probability distributions of key parameters, attend to correlated inputs (do not assume independence), use expert elicitation (Delphi or structured methods) where appropriate, and portray probabilistic results meaningfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report expected values and distributional information
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide expected-value estimates as well as distributions about the estimates where information exists; when providing bounds, use 95% and 5% confidence bounds where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasis on expected values is appropriate under assumed risk neutrality; if adopting different risk preferences, explain reasons. Detailed reporting of distributions is not required but should be available on request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of benefits and costs over time (discounting and presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present undiscounted streams of benefit and cost estimates for each year of the analytic time horizon and annualized benefits and costs using real discount rates of 3% and 7%. Report all monetized effects in 2001 dollars using the GDP deflator to convert from other years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start annualized streams in the year the final rule begins to have effects; report both undiscounted and annualized streams; use both 3% and 7% real discount rates to show sensitivity to discounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and rounding of estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported estimates should reflect the precision of the analysis; rounding conveys implied precision (e.g., $220M implies +/- $5M if rounded to nearest $10M).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose rounding that matches analytic precision and avoid implying spurious accuracy; document the implied precision and rounding conventions used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid double-counting and correctly classify transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid double-counting effects and report transfers separately; distinguish transfers from net welfare gains to society and between 'on-budget' and 'off-budget' transfers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use categories as necessary to describe redistributive effects; if transfers have efficiency effects in addition to distributional effects, report them separately. Ensure costs/savings are not double-counted in numerator and denominator of ratios or CE calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include all relevant costs to society
rubrics_metrics.description: When measuring costs, include all relevant costs to society—public and private—and subtract cost savings where appropriate to obtain net costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For CEA numerator, reflect net costs = gross compliance costs minus cost savings; avoid reducing gross costs by monetized benefits already used in denominator effectiveness measures (avoid double-counting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate effectiveness metrics for public health and safety
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying CEA to public health and safety rulemakings, select measures of effectiveness (lives saved, life-years, QALYs, ELs) that permit comparisons of alternatives and account for morbidity as well as mortality where relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain choice of effectiveness measure; prefer integrated measures when rule significantly impacts both mortality and morbidity; be aware of underlying assumptions (e.g., QALY assumptions) and fairness implications; report multiple measures when useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness and treatment of population subgroups
rubrics_metrics.description: When making numeric adjustments for life expectancy or quality-of-life, prefer population averages rather than subgroup averages dominated by particular demographic or income groups; ensure fair treatment of all segments when adjusting effectiveness measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a rule saves lives in populations with disabilities, do not necessarily diminish life-years saved based on subgroup disability rates; explain adjustments and use representative averages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardized accounting statement and reporting categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an accounting statement with tables reporting benefit and cost estimates for each major final rule, reporting benefits and costs within three categories: monetized, quantified but not monetized, and qualitative (not quantified or monetized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use provided suggested format (tables with primary/minimum/maximum estimates and source citations); present annualized monetized costs and benefits and qualitative descriptions for unquantified effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate reporting of effects on groups and economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify portions of benefits, costs, and transfers received by State, local, and tribal governments; where feasible, identify effects on small businesses, wages, and economic growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that rules with annual costs below $1 billion are likely to have minimal effect on economic growth; use as many categories as necessary to describe major redistributive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Flexibility Act / small entity analysis (RFA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Regulatory Flexibility Act, prepare a proposed and final regulatory flexibility analysis (RFA) if the rule could have a significant impact on a substantial number of small entities; consult agency guidelines and SBA Office of Advocacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post RFAs online for public review; notify Chief Counsel for Advocacy of draft rules with significant economic impacts on small entities per EO 13272; incorporate SBREFA procedures (EPA/OSHA consult) where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfunded Mandates Act compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Unfunded Mandates Act, prepare a written statement about benefits and costs prior to issuing a proposed or final rule that may result in aggregate expenditures of $100,000,000 or more in any one year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical requirements under EO 12866 are similar and may satisfy this requirement; ensure explicit consideration and documentation when thresholds are exceeded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the rulemaking will create information collection, paperwork, or recordkeeping burdens; OMB approval is required for new collections imposed on 10 or more persons and a valid OMB control number must be obtained for any covered paperwork.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify the practical utility of any required information for implementation; consult agency CIO for compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information quality standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Data and analysis used to support proposed and final rules must meet agency and OMB information quality standards (Information Quality Law and implementing guidelines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with agency CIO and OMB Statistical and Science Policy Branch for assistance; ensure minimum quality standards for regulatory analysis are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEPA and environmental impact considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Comply with NEPA: consider environmental impacts of agency decisions and complete NEPA documentation (environmental impact statement for major Federal actions significantly affecting the human environment) before issuing a final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow CEQ regulations (40 C.F.R. 1500-1508) and associated guidance; coordinate NEPA analysis with regulatory analysis where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impacts on children (EO 13045)
rubrics_metrics.description: For economically significant rules concerning environmental health or safety risks that may disproportionately affect children, provide an evaluation of environmental health or safety effects on children and explain why the planned regulation is preferable to reasonably feasible alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address disproportionate risks to children to the extent permitted by law and consistent with agency mission; include required OMB/OIRA evaluation where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy impacts (EO 13211)
rubrics_metrics.description: For significant energy actions, prepare and submit to OMB a Statement of Energy Effects describing any adverse effects on energy supply, distribution, or use and the effects of reasonable alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish the Statement or a summary in the NPRM and final rule; consult OMB Memorandum 01-27 for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption against certain economic regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a presumption against price controls in competitive markets, production/sales quotas in competitive markets, mandatory uniform quality standards if voluntary measures suffice, and controls on entry into employment or production except in narrow circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A particularly demanding burden of proof is required to justify such regulations; exceptions exist (e.g., indispensable health/safety requirements or management of common property resources).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider non-regulatory and lower-level alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Before federal regulation, consider alternatives such as antitrust enforcement, consumer litigation, administrative compensation systems, State/local regulation, and informational or market-based measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether State/local solutions, experimentation, or harmonization with international rules would better address the problem; evaluate possibility of reducing State/local regulation where fragmentation imposes national costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for performance standards and market-oriented approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally prefer performance standards (outcomes-based) over design standards (prescriptive) and explore market-oriented approaches (fees, subsidies, tradable permits, changes in liability/property rights) where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for cost savings from flexibility and costs of ensuring compliance (monitoring); examples include averaging, banking, and trading programs with attention to local 'hot spots.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate informational remedies when information failures exist
rubrics_metrics.description: If market failure arises from inadequate or asymmetric information, evaluate informational measures (standardized testing/rating systems, mandatory disclosure, government provision of information) as often preferred to prescriptive regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate costs (gathering/communicating info, displacement of other info, misinterpretation) and consider least intrusive informational alternative sufficient to accomplish objectives; where feasible, consider voluntary standard-setting backed by government testing/rating systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency across agencies and comparability of analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain analytical consistency in estimating benefits and costs across regulations and agencies to allow comparison and achieve most risk reduction for a given resource level, subject to statutory limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent valuation methods, reporting formats, discounting conventions, and clearly explain deviations due to statutory constraints or unique circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple measures and present alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB encourages agencies to report results with multiple measures of effectiveness and benefit valuation when useful to provide different insights and perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain which measures were selected and why, present alternative primary estimates for key valuations (e.g., mortality risk valuation), and provide sensitivity to those choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misleading ratio-based decision rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on benefit-cost ratios or average cost-effectiveness ratios as the sole decision metric because they can be misleading; focus on net benefits and incremental comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using CEA, present incremental cost-effectiveness ratios comparing successively more stringent options and eliminate alternatives dominated by strong/weak dominance principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation of models and appendices
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide appendices with documentation of models and detailed data when necessary to allow replication and evaluation by qualified third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include model descriptions, data sources, calibration, and any computer code or equations essential to replication; make detailed uncertainty analysis available upon request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early and ongoing stakeholder consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek opinions of those affected by the regulation and of individuals/organizations with relevant knowledge early and throughout the analysis to ensure relevant issues are addressed and data obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not limit consultation to final stages; early consultation improves analysis quality and data access. Consider SBREFA and other stakeholder engagement requirements where applicable.
